content: Nitrofurantoin is indicated for the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs) caused by susceptible bacteria, including Escherichia coli, Enterococcus species, Enterobacter species, Klebsiella species, Staphylococcus aureus, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus. For macrocrystal formulations (e.g., Macrodantin, Furadantin suspension, and equivalents), the recommended dosage is 50–100 mg orally every 6 hours for 7 days or for 3 days after obtaining sterile urine. For monohydrate/macrocrystal formulations (e.g., Macrobid and equivalents), the recommended dosage is 100 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 days or for 3 days after obtaining sterile urine. For long-term prophylaxis or suppression, 50–100 mg of macrocrystals can be taken orally at bedtime for up to 12 months. Nitrofurantoin is not indicated for the treatment of pyelonephritis or perinephric abscesses. It is approved for use in patients aged one month or older with UTIs caused by susceptible bacteria. Drug Interactions: 1. BCG Vaccine (Live): Nitrofurantoin decreases the effects of the BCG vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is complete. This interaction is contraindicated. 2. Cholera Vaccine: Avoid coadministration with systemic antibiotics, as they may inactivate the vaccine strain. Do not administer the cholera vaccine to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 3. Darolutamide: This drug increases nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP). Avoid coadministration or monitor closely for adverse reactions, and consider dose adjustments of nitrofurantoin. 4. Enasidenib: This drug increases nitrofurantoin levels by affecting BCRP and other transporters. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs. If unavoidable, reduce the dosage of nitrofurantoin substrates as per prescribing information. 5. Lasmiditan: This drug increases nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting BCRP. Avoid coadministration with BCRP substrates. 6. Lenolisib: This drug increases nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting BCRP. Avoid coadministration or use alternative drugs. 7. Calcium Carbonate, Aluminum Hydroxide, Magnesium Compounds (e.g., magnesium chloride, citrate, hydroxide, oxide, sulfate): These agents decrease nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Separate administration by at least 2 hours. 8. Estradiol, Ethinyl Estradiol, Conjugated Estrogens, Levonorgestrel, Mestranol, and Other Hormonal Contraceptives: Nitrofurantoin may decrease the effectiveness of these agents by altering intestinal flora. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 9. Digoxin: Nitrofurantoin may increase digoxin levels by altering intestinal flora. Monitor closely. 10. Dapsone (Topical): Nitrofurantoin may increase the risk of methemoglobinemia when coadministered. Monitor closely and modify therapy if necessary. 11. Didanosine: This drug increases nitrofurantoin levels by raising gastric pH. Administer nitrofurantoin 2 hours before or several hours after didanosine. 12. Fostemsavir, Glecaprevir/Pibrentasvir, Tafamidis, and Other BCRP Inhibitors: These drugs may increase nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Monitor closely and consider dose adjustments. 13. Metoclopramide: This drug decreases nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Monitor closely. 14. Microbiota Oral (Probiotics): Nitrofurantoin may reduce the efficacy of probiotics containing bacterial spores. Complete antibiotic therapy 2–4 days before initiating probiotics. 15. Pexidartinib: This drug may increase the risk of hepatotoxicity when coadministered with nitrofurantoin. Avoid coadministration or monitor liver function tests (LFTs) closely. 16. Sodium Bicarbonate and Sodium Citrate/Citric Acid: These agents decrease nitrofurantoin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Separate administration by at least 2 hours. 17. Valoctocogene Roxaparvovec: Coadministration with nitrofurantoin may increase the risk of hepatotoxicity. Monitor liver enzymes closely and consider alternative medications. 18. Thiamine, Biotin, Pyridoxine, Pantothenic Acid: Nitrofurantoin may decrease the levels of these vitamins by altering intestinal flora. Monitor closely, though the clinical significance is unknown. Special Considerations: Nitrofurantoin is contraindicated for use with live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine) during active antibiotic therapy. Monitor for potential adverse effects when nitrofurantoin is coadministered with drugs that inhibit BCRP or alter intestinal flora. Adjust dosages of nitrofurantoin or interacting drugs as necessary to minimize toxicity or therapeutic failure.
